_note: Scored experiments are families of workload instances drawn from the paper's own evaluation settings (Sections 4.2-4.3). Each method is run as a solver on every instance under a 120 CPU-second budget per instance (the paper's 120 s solver limit, counted by the evaluator as CPU time); train instances are public (eval/train/instances.json), test instances are held out. The family means are not quantities the paper reports, so the paper's numbers are kept under '_' keys (per experiment and in '_paper_reported') and as labelled anchors rather than as results the gym must match. Setup scaling: 10-12 instances per family per slice instead of the paper's full sweeps; otherwise node counts, optical degrees, bandwidths (800/k Gbps), base latency (20 us) and switching latencies follow the paper.

allreduce_scaling.description: Paper Fig. 8(a) setting: Rabenseifner AllReduce on 64-1024 nodes (12-20 steps), k=4 optical planes at 200 Gbps, 16-64 MB payloads, 20 us base latency, 200 us reconfiguration latency; switching share of the lockstep time 0.35-0.80.

cct_reduction_vs_strawman_pct.description: Mean over the family's instances of the percent full-collective completion-time reduction versus the lockstep Strawman-ICR schedule computed by the evaluator (per instance clipped to [-100, 100]). A failed run scores -100.

valid_schedule.description: 1 if every instance of every experiment got a physically valid schedule within the CPU budget (traffic conservation, plane indices < k, alpha-beta transmission time, switching latency, per-plane serial use, step barriers); 0 for a failed run.

allreduce_scaling._paper_note: Anchor: the paper's Fig. 8(a) reduction over Strawman-ICR at 64 nodes (32 MB, k=4), 39.6%, growing to 46.9% at 512 nodes. The scored value is a mean over 64-1024 nodes and 16-64 MB payloads, which the paper does not report; the anchor is a paper point, not a target.

high_optical_degree.description: Paper Fig. 7(a)-(b) setting: Rabenseifner ReduceScatter and AllReduce on 128-1024 nodes with k=8 optical planes at 100 Gbps, 1-512 MB payloads, 200 us reconfiguration latency; switching share 0.35-0.92. Bruck and Pairwise All-to-All at k=8 are not scored (see scoring/EXPERIMENTS.md).

high_optical_degree._paper_note: The paper reports k=8 results for these algorithms only as peaks over a message-size sweep ('up to' 89.1% for ReduceScatter and 87.1% for AllReduce), kept under '_paper_fig7_peak_*' with the two unscored All-to-All peaks. Anchor (swot): the paper's only non-peak AllReduce reduction, 46.9% (Fig. 8(a), 512 nodes, k=4) - same algorithm, lower optical degree. The family mean is not reported by the paper; the anchor is not a target.

hardware_sensitivity.description: Paper Section 4.3 setting: 256-node Rabenseifner/Bruck collectives and 9- or 17-node Pairwise All-to-All with optical degree k in {2,4,8} at 800/k Gbps and reconfiguration latency in {0.02, 0.2, 2, 20} ms (every algorithm once per k at k=2 and k=4, Rabenseifner only at k=8), payloads 0.25-8192 MB chosen around the transmission/switching knee (switching share 0.35-0.92).

hardware_sensitivity._paper_note: Section 4.3 reports robustness only graphically (Figs. 10-11), noting that at k=8 the 120 s solver limit can give sub-optimal schedules. Anchor (swot): the paper's Fig. 8(a) AllReduce reduction at k=4 and 0.2 ms switching - one grid point of this sweep - 46.9% at 512 nodes (39.6% at 64 nodes). The paper's 8-node k=2 design example (1500 -> 1200 us, 20%) is kept under '_paper_fig5_8node_k2'. The sweep mean is not reported by the paper; the anchor is not a target.

_paper_reported._note: The paper's reported numbers, unchanged from earlier iterations. The three named instances are reproduced as unscored experiments in scoring/scores.json.

_weights_note: Weights 0.4/0.3/0.3 (iteration 12): the paper's headline quantitative claim is cluster scalability (Fig. 8(a): 39.6% -> 46.9%); algorithm-level efficiency at high optical degree (Fig. 7) and robustness to optical degree and switching latency (Section 4.3, Figs. 10-11) are the other two evaluation axes. The k=8 family now covers two of Fig. 7's four algorithms, and the hardware sweep now separates a stronger scheduler from the reference (it was down-weighted to 0.2 in iteration 11 because it did not).
